records.title: (clubbed) GUIDELINES FOR APPROVAL OF FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN PRINT MEDIA .
details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether Government have fixed any guidelines for the approval of foreign 
investment in print media; and 
(b) if so, the details of such guidelines and whether the proposal of foreign 
investment would be considered in the light of these guidelines or the procedure 
of taking decision on case to case basis would be followed?

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SMT. SUSHMA SWARAJ)
(a) & (b):
The Government have issued guidelines for approval of proposals for publication 
of Indian editions of foreign scientific, technical and speciality magazines/periodicals/journals and for foreign investment upto 74% in Indian entities publishing scientific, technical and speciality magazines/periodicals/journals. A copy of the guidelines is at Annexure. Guidelines regarding FDI in News and Current Affairs have not been issued so far.
ANNEXURE TO PART b) OF THE RAJYA SABHA UNSTARRED QUESTION 
NO.86 FOR ANSWER ON 18.11.2002 GUIDELINES FOR:
(i) PUBLICATION OF INDIAN EDITIONS OF FOREIGN TECHNICAL/SCIENTIFIC/SPECIALITY 
MAGAZINES/JOURNALS/PERIODICALS; AND 
(ii) FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN INDIAN ENTITIES PUBLISHING 
SCIENTIFIC/TECHNICAL/SPECIALITY MAGAZINES/JOURNALS/PERIODICALS
PREAMBLE
 The Union Government has decided to allow: 
(i) publication of Indian editions of foreign scientific, technical and speciality 
magazines/periodicals/journals; and 
(ii) foreign investment upto 74% in Indian entities publishing scientific/technical 
and speciality magazines/periodicals/journals. 
1. Application
(i) An application shall be made to the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting 
in the prescribed format to determine the nature of contents of the publication 
(ii) Application fee of Rs. 5000/- (Rupees Five thousand only) shall have to be 
deposited through a Demand Draft in favour of the Pay & Accounts Officer, 
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, payable at New Delhi.
2. Processing
(i) The application shall be processed by the Ministry of I&B, after due inter-
Ministerial consultations, to decide whether the proposed publication is 
covered under the category of scientific, technical or speciality 
magazine/periodical/journal. Representatives of the concerned 
Ministries/specialist bodies and language experts, as found necessary will be 
associated in this task. In appropriate cases, the Ministry of I&B will issue:
a) An approval, subject to compliance with the provisions of the 
Press and Registration of Books Act and Rules made thereunder 
for publication of the foreign journal; or
b) A No Objection Certificate (NOC) for foreign investment, a copy 
of which would be sent to RNI/SIA/RBI and the applicant. 
(ii) Determination of category assigned to the publication(s) is liable for review 
by the Ministry of I&B if the contents of the publication(s) undergo change at 
a later date. 
(iii) a) In cases where both FDI and FII investment is envisaged, the 
applicant may approach the FIPB/RBI for clearance after obtaining the No 
Objection Certificate from the Ministry of I&B.
b) In cases involving only portfolio investment, the applicant may 
approach the Reserve Bank of India, for further clearance, if any, 
after obtaining the No Objection Certificate from the Ministry of 
I&B.
c) The Ministry of I&B will keep the Secretariat for Industrial 
Assistance and the Reserve Bank of India informed of the FDI 
projected by the Company and the balance permissible foreign 
investment on the portfolio investment route, while communicating 
the No Objection. 
3. Title of the Publication
Title verification shall continue to be done by the Press Registrar as per 
existing procedure.
4. Foreign Investment 
(i) Total foreign investment upto 74% may be allowed. Guidelines of the 
Ministry of Finance on FDI and portfolio investment would apply subject to 
the overall ceiling of 74% mentioned above. 
(ii) All cases involving Foreign Investment shall be handled by the prescribed 
agencies, viz. FDI on the government approval route through the mechanism 
of the FIPB and portfolio investment by the RBI.

records.title: ELECTRICITY GENERATED BY VARIOUS FUELS .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that water, nuclear energy, coal, naphtha, oil, gas 
and husk of sugarcane are used fuel for generation of electricity in the 
country;
(b) if not the different kinds of material used for generating electricity 
during March, 2000 to March, 2002; and
(c) the average cost of electricity generated by each of the above 
mentioned material used?

THE MINISTER OF POWER
( SHRI SURESH PRABHU )
(a) to (c) : A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.
 STATEMENT
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (c) OF 
STARRED QUESTION NO. 341 TO BE ANSWERED IN THE RAJYA 
SABHA ON 07.08.2002 REGARDING ELECTRICITY GENERATED 
BY VARIOUS FUELS.
(a) to (c) : Electricity in India is generated through various sources, such as, 
coal, hydro, gas, diesel, nuclear etc. Electricity is also available through 
renewable sources like wind, solar photovoltaic, biomass, energy from wastes, etc.
 As on 31.03.2002, the installed capacity from various sources was as 
follows: -
Type of Fuel Installed Capacity (MW) 
Hydro 26261.22
Coal 62130.89 
Diesel 1134.83
Gas 11163.10
Nuclear 2720.00
Wind 1507.46
Solar Photovoltaic 54 MW
Small Hydro (upto 25 MW) 1437 MW 
Biomass Cogeneration 381 MW
Biomass Gassifier 51 MW
Energy recovery from wastes 22 MW
 The per unit cost of generation of power from various sources (2000-
01) was as follows :
Source Paisa/Kwh
Coal 151
Hydro 63
Gas 220
Naphtha 506
Nuclear 82 – 295
Wind 225 – 275
Small Hydro 200 – 250
Biomass Power/Bagasse co-generation 150 – 275 
Waste to energy 250 – 350
Solar Photovoltaic (depending upon size configuration, 
location etc.) 1200 - 2000
 All India weighted average.
 The Government has undertaken a number of measures for 
accelerating the pace of hydropower development in the country with the ultimate 
objective of fully developing the feasible hydro potential in the country, as this is a 
renewable source of energy with no fuel cost. As can be seen from the above 
table, the cost of generation from coal is quite low. The cost of generation from 
nuclear sources is expected to come down over time to international levels as the 
plans for having 20,000 MW of nuclear capacity by 2020 are implemented. Gas 
and Naphtha are relatively costly options.
 The following are the salient features of the comprehensive strategy 
evolved for the full development of the hydro potential in the country: -
? Central Electricity Authority has completed a ranking study of all the 
identified hydro potential sites in the major river basins of the country. 
This ranking study forms the basis for prioritizing the development of the 
hydro sites.
? Active role of the states in selection, prioritization and monitoring of 
execution of projects specially in view of the critical responsibility of the 
States in land acquisition and rehabilitation and resettlement.
? In pursuance of the ranking study an International Round Table is being 
organized where developers, countries with strength in hydro power 
development, multi lateral agencies and financial institutions would be 
invited with the objective of identifying projects for the preparation of 
DPRs and subsequent development.
? A Committee has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri Harish 
Salve, Solicitor General of India to suggest ways and means for increasing 
transparency and streamlining contract management in hydro projects. This 
is aimed at reduction in time and cost over runs associated with hydro 
projects and in turn to lower capital costs.
? A Three Stage clearance process for new hydro projects has been 
introduced. This facilitates thorough preparation of DPRs so as to 
minimize possibilities of geological surprises with land acquisition and 
proper development of infrastructure including roads and bridges being 
done in parallel after establishment of feasibility and commercial viability 
of a project. Development of necessary infrastructure before award of 
major contract packages is expected to result in reduction of the gestation 
period of hydro projects and consequently lower costs.
? An effective system of review of catchment area treatment as well as 
compensatory afforestation has been introduced. In addition, a Special 
Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for compensatory afforestation has been planned 
which would create a land bank from which credits could be taken for large 
power projects. These measures are designed to take care of environmental 
concerns relating to large hydro projects.

details:
(a) whether Government have made an assessment of expenditure incurred on transmission 
and distribution of power;
(b) if so, the amount being spent per unit by electricity boards in each State on transmission 
and distribution of electricity;
(c) whether it is also a fact that the said amount of expenditure is much more than the 
amount of expenditure incurred at international level; and
(d) if so, the average expenditure at international level?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
( SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA )
(a) & (b) : According to the Annual Report of the Planning Commission on the Working of 
State Electricity Boards (SEBs) and Electricity Departments (EDs) (June, 2002), the outlay on 
transmission & distribution in various States during the period 1992-93 to 2000-2001 is 
enclosed as Annex. The per unit cost of transmission varies according to the location of the 
generating stations, quantum of power flows apart from the investments made.
(c) & (d) : It may not be appropriate to compare the investment made on transmission and 
distribution in our country with that of other countries. The transmission & distribution system in 
our country is still at the developmental stage wherein large areas are still required to be 
electrified and hence huge investment is required in this sector. 
 As per the report of Rajyadhaksha Committee on Power (1980), the thumb rule for 
investment ratio of expenditure on generation, Transmission & Distribution and rural 
electrification should be 4:2:1:1 between generation on one hand and the transmission and 
distribution (including rural electrification) on the other. The actual ratio of investment on 
generation and Transmission & Distribution (including RE) has been less than 1:1 except during 
the first plan period as adequate resources were not available for investment on system 
improvement schemes.

records.title: RAIN WATER HARVESTING RESERVES .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that there is ample rain water available
 in the country;
(b) if so, whether rain water harvesting reserves have been set
up in each State of the country; and
(c) if so, the storage capacity of each of the rain water
harvesting reserves set up in each of such States in the country
?

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI) 
(a) India receives an average annual precipitation of 4000
Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) which includes rainfall and snow. Out
of this, 3,000 BCM occurs during monsoon. The average annual flow
in various rivers of the country is assessed at 1869 BCM. Out of
this, utilizable flow by conventional methods is estimated at 690
BCM. In addition about 200-250 BCM can be utilised through inter-
basin water transfer from the surplus river basins to the deficit
water basins. 
(b) & (c) No, Sir. Water being a State subject, it is for the
concerned State Government to take steps in this regard. The
Ministry of Water Resources has, however, circulated a Manual on
Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to the States/Union
Territories to enable them to formulate area specific artificial
recharge scheme to check the declining trend in ground water
levels. State-wise estimated availability of rain water for
ground water recharge, as assessed by the Central Ground Water
Board, is given in the enclosed Statement.

records.title: DECLINE IN BASIC AMENITIES IN METROPOLITAN CITIES
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that the basic amenities are
 declining day by day in metropolitan cities due to continuous
 increase in the population;
(b) if so, whether any assessment has been made regarding
 the lack of drinking water, sanitation,schools, electricity and
 transportation in these cities; and
(c) if so, the details in this regard, city-wise?

MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT & POVERTY ALLEVIATION
( SHRI ANANTH KUMAR )
(a),(b)&(c): A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha.
.PA
STATEMENT
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO RAJYA SABHA STARRED QUESTION
NO.204 FOR 29.7.2002 REGARDING DECLINE IN BASIC AMENITIES IN
METROPOLITAN CITIES.
.SP2
The number of metropolitan cities and urban
agglomerations has increased from 23 in 1991 to 35 in 2001. The
population in these cities has also grown from 70,996,726 in
1991 to 107,813,906 in 2001 as per the Census of India.
Consequently, there has been pressure on the basic amenities in
the Metropolitan Cities. The development of urban
infrastructure by the cities have not kept pace with the growth
in population.
As per Entry Nos. 6 & 17 of List II - State List of the
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, public health,
sanitation & water supply are the responsibility of the State
Governments. Central Government, however, supplements the
efforts of State Governments through policy formulation,
technical guidance & Central assistance through the Centrally
Sponsored Schemes for urban infrastructure development in the
areas of water supply, sanitation & urban transportation. The
Central Government also assists State Governments in development
of urban infrastructure with the support of
multinational/bilateral agencies.
As per study conducted by the Central Pollution Control
Board in 1994-95, the 23 metro cities (as per 1991 census) had
per capita drinking water supply availability ranging from 74
Litres Per Capita Per Day (lpcd) in Madurai upto 341 lpcd in
Delhi. Within a City, there has been variation in the
availability of drinking water from area to area. City-wise
details are at Annexure.
National Institute of Urban Affairs has been entrusted
with a study to assess the status of water supply, sanitation
and solid waste management in 300 cities & towns, including the
metropolitan cities. The report is yet to be finalized.

details:
(THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENTS OF ATOMIC ENERGY AND SPACE. (SMT.VASUNDHARA RAJE)
(a)&(b): The Central Vigilance Commission(CVC) has not identified any Department of the Government as area of corruption.
(c)&(d): The Government is fully alive to ensure the corruption free functioning of the Government Departments. Polices in this regard have been formulated and constantly monitored for their effective implementation. Necessary modifications are also carried out from time to time in order to make them more effective and responsive to the needs of a changing environment. The Government has also set up Information and Facilitation Counters (IFCs) in various Ministries/Departments to provide information regarding procedures and schemes of concerned organizations to ensure greater transparency and for eliminating corruption. Besides, the Secretary of the concerned Department, assisted by Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO), is made responsible for ensuring probity and integrity in that Department.

records.title: (clubbed) GROWTH IN HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT .
details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether it is a fact that the rate of human resource development in the States has been 
distinct in the country during nineties; 
(b) if so, what has been the annual rate of human resource development in each of the States 
during nineties;
(c) whether it is also a fact that the rate of human resource development in those States has 
been more where per capita income is more; and
(d) if not, the facts in this regard?
 ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES,

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES 
AND PENSIONS, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING AND 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENTS OF ATOMIC ENERGY AND SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE)
(a) & (b): The National Human Development Report (NHDR) – 2001 prepared by the 
Planning Commission and released by the Prime Minister on April 23rd, 2002 has presented a 
Human Development Index (HDI) for all States and UTs for the early eighties (using data for 
1981 to 1983) and the early nineties (using data for 1991 to 1993-94) and only for major States 
for 2001 due to the non-availability, so far, of the required data for all States/UTs from the 
Census 2001. The Report does not separately estimate yearly rates of growth in human 
development.
(c) & (d): From the analysis it turns out that for the economically better off States, as well as 
for the poor States, attainments on HDI and income levels show a direct correspondence. In other 
words, the poor States are also the States with relatively poor performance on HDI. Similarly, the 
economically better-off States are also the ones with relatively better performance on the HDI. 
However, the relation between the HDI and the level of development does not show any 
correspondence among the middle-income States.

(a) for the companies having no profits or inadequate profits, limits under schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been revised. 
(b) Based on effective capital of the company, earlier limits were Rs.75,000/- to Rs.2,00,000/- per month. These have now been revised to Rs.1,50,000/- to Rs.4,00,000/- per month and linked to good corporate governance practices.
(c) The decision was taken as a liberalizing measure and to encourage good corporate governance. The inflation that has taken place since the previous limits were fixed, was also taken into consideration.

records.title: MODIFIED STUDENTS COMPUTER PROGRAMME .
details:
(a) whether Government have decided to started
 computer education system in 60,000 schools under
 modified Students Computer Programme, to provide
 computer education in the country ;
(b) if so in which States, these 60,000 schools have
 been selected, giving the State wise number
 thereof; and
(c) the average number of students who would get
 computer education annually in these schools?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(PROF. RITA VERMA)
(a) to (c): The Department of Secondary and Higher
Education has launched a revised Computer Literacy and
Studies in Schools (CLASS) scheme to impart computer
education to the students of Government and Government
aided schools. Under the scheme. financial
assistance is being provided to State/Uts on the basis
of Computer Education Plans (CEPs) submitted by the
States/Uts. Besides the KVS and NVS would convert one
school per State/UT into a SMART school for which a
grant of not more than Rs.25 Lakhs would be given per
SMART school. Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya
Vidyalayas would also be given funds at the rate of
Rs.15,000/- per neighbourhood school to impart
computer literacy to 10 neighbourhood school to cover
10,000 such schools over a period of three years.
So far, nineteen States/Uts have been released
funds under the scheme, on the basis of CEPs submitted by
them. the names of States/Uts and the number of schools 
which have been granted financial assistance under the 
revised CLASS scheme is Annexed.

records.title: COMMERCIAL PRODUCTION OF NEW SEEDS .
details:
(a) whether Government have made any permanent arrangement for commercial 
production of new seeds of foodgrains developed during the past few years; 
(b) if so, the details of this arrangement together with the names of the seeds which 
have been made available for commercial production under this arrangement, during the 
last three yeas; and
(c) the average annual quantum of availability of such seeds?

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV)
(a): Yes, Sir.
(b)&(c): Indents for production of breeder seeds of newly developed varieties are given to 
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR ) for production. The breeder seed so 
produced is allotted to various seed producing Agencies for further multiplication and 
commercial production. The crop-wise quantity of breeder seed allotted for multiplication 
during the last three years is enclosed at Annexure-I. The crop and variety-wise quantity of 
certified and quality seeds made available for commercial production during last three years 
is enclosed at Annexure-II.

records.title: MONITORING MECHANISM FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF PMGY .
details:
(a) whether Government have also set up any monitoring mechanism for effective 
implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana;
(b) If so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the States where this mechanism has already been set up ?

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES & PENSIONS, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY 
OF PLANNING AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENTS OF 
ATOMIC ENERGY AND SPACE
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE)
(a): Yes, Sir.
(b) and (c): Both physical and financial monitoring of Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya 
Yojana (PMGY) were being carried out by the concerned central ministries as per the 
guidelines issued by them. This was applicable to all the States, since the PMGY is 
being implemented in the entire country. 
Planning Commission intends to directly monitor PMGY from the current 
year 2002-03.

Because of the persistent efforts of the Employees Provident Fund Organization, an amount of Rs.858 crore was collected during the year 2001-2002.

details:
(a) whether the responsibility for making the entire wasteland in the 
country cultivable has ben entrusted to an institute by Government by 
integrating all the existing plans;
(b) if so, the name of such institute and the reasons for giving preference
to the above institute for such responsibility; and
(c) by when the wasteland is targeted to be made cultivable together 
with the area o the same?

MINISTER OF STATE FOR RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL)
a) No Sir.
b) Question does not arise.
c) As per Wastelands Atlas of India 2000 (brought out by the Department 
of Land Rsources in Collaboration with National Remote Sensing Agency, Hyderabad
employing Satellit Remote Sensing Technologies), the total extent of wastelands in 
the country is 63.85 m. ha. Wastelands are degraded lands, which are currently
under-utilized and are deteriorating for lack of appropriat water and soil
management or on account of natural cuases. Therefore, agricultural operations
are gnerally not feasible on such lands at the first stage of development. 
The Department of Land Resources has the mandate to develop wastelands rather 
than to convert wastelands into cultivable lands. It is implementing three
major Schemes viz. the Integrated Wastelands Development programme (IWDP), 
the Drought Prone Areas Progrmme (DPAP) and the Desert Development Programme 
(DDP)for development of wstelands/degrded lands on watershed basis w.e.f. 
1.4.1995. New projects covering 139.73 lac hectares have been taken up under 
these Schemes from 1.4.95 to 31.3.2002.

records.title: (clubbed) TAXES ON PROCESSING OF COTTON AND READY MADE GARMENTS
details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether it is a fact that taxes have been levied by 
 Government at many levels from the process of cotton 
 production to that of manufacturing of readymade garments;
(b) if so, the details of those taxes and their rates levied at
 present; and
(c) the likely increase in the pricing of the readymade garments 
 following the tax determination percentage-wise?

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
 (SHRI GINGEE N.RAMACHANDRAN)
(a), (b) & (c): A statement is laid on the Table of the House.
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PART (A), (B) AND (C) OF 
RAJYA SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 592 TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 
7TH MAY, 2002.
(a): Excise duty is levied by the Central Government at the stage 
of manufacture of cotton yarn, cotton fabrics and ready-made 
garments of cotton. 
(b): Details of excise duties levied on cotton textiles and textile
products are as given below:-
(1) Cotton yarn - 9.2% ad valorem [ 8% Basic Excise duty (BED)+ 15% 
of BED as Additional Excise Duty (Textiles and Textile Articles);
(2) Cotton fabrics - 12% ad valorem [8% BED + 4% Additional Excise
Duty in lieu of sales tax]
(3) Cotton ready made garments - 12% ad valorem
However, CENVAT credit of the basic excise duty paid at the earlier 
stage can be availed for discharging duty liability at the subsequent
stages in the production chain. Thus there is no cascading effect of 
excise duties on account of imposition of duty at various stages of
manufacture. Further in the case of readymade garments, exemption 
from excise duty is available for small scale units upto a turnover 
limit of Rs. One crore in a year subject to certain conditions. 
Clothing accessories and undergarments are, however, fully exempt
from excise duty.
(c): Prices of ready made garments are determined by market forces. 
The impact of excise duty on the prices of ready made garments 
is limited to the value addition at the garment manufacturing 
stage.

details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

 utilised in the country at present;

out of the total quantity of water utilised;
(c) the quantity of underground water as well as ground water
being utilised at present for irrigation purpose; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES

(a) & (b) The total water use, as in the year 2000, was estimated
to be 605 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) per annum for all kinds of
uses. Out of this, it was estimated that water use for
agriculture was 501 BCM which works out to 84% of the total water

the ground water levels in certain parts of the country due to
over-exploitation of ground water.

records.title: (clubbed) APPOINTMENT OF JUDGES ON POPULATION BASIS
details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY) 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Both the Government and the judiciary are concerned with the insufficient number
of judges. The Judge strength in the High Courts is reviewed once in three years. The 
Judge strength in the District/Subordinate Court is worked out on the basis of yardsticks 
fixed by the concerned High Courts. The posts of
Judges/Judicial Officers along-with supporting staff are created by the concerned State 
Governments. These posts are also filled up by the concerned State Govemments/UT
Administration/High Courts as per their rules and procedure. 
(c) At present, there is one judge for a population of 74,571. 
(d) The Eleventh Law Commission in its 120th Report on `Manpower Planning in Judiciary: 
A Blue Print` in July, 1987, has recommended that the present strength of 10.5 Judges per 
million population be increased to 50 Judges per million population in a phased manner. 
The 120th Report of the Law Commission which had recommended increase in the number of 
Judicial Officers was circulated amongst all the State Govemments/UT Administrations/
High Courts for necessary action at their end.
The Department-related Parliamentry Standing Committee on Home Affairs in its 85th Report 
on `Law`s Delays: Arrears in Courts` has endorsed the Law Commission`s recommendations and 
suggested that variations can be made for different jurisdictions on the basis of pendency, 
rate of disposal and other relevant factors in consultation with the judiciary.
The Supreme court in its judgment dated 21.3.2002 in W.P.(Civil) No. 1022/89. All India 
Judges Association Vs. Union of India & others has suggested that the increase in the 
judge strength to 50 judges per 10 lakh people should be effected and implemented with 
the filling up of the posts in a phased manner to be determined and directed by the Union
Ministry of Law, but this process should be completed and the increased vacancies and 
posts filled within a period of five years from today.

Besides, there are around six lakh Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathic doctors registered with their respective Councils. The norm for availability of doctors to the population in the country, has been recommended to be as 1:2000 by the Bhore Committee. 4% in this sector. The installed capacity for processing of
fruits and vegetables at the end of the 9th Five Year Plan in
the organized sector has been 21.5 lakh tonnes. The Ministry
of Food processing Industries is operating plan schemes to
provide financial incentives to the food processing
industries. The schemes are :
Scheme for Infrastructure Development.
Scheme for Technology Up-gradation, establishment and
Modernization of Food processing Industries.
Scheme for Quality Assurance, Codex Standards and
Research & Development.
Scheme for Human Resources Development.
Scheme for strengthening of institutions.
For the Tenth Plan an allocation of Rs. 650 crores has
been earmarked for the operation of the schemes of the
Ministry. The growth in the fruit & vegetable processing
sector is projected at 8.9% if GDP grows at 6% per annum
during the Tenth Plan. In case GDP grows at 8% as per the
approach paper of the Planning Commission, the likely growth
in this sector is projected at 11.7%. The installed capacity
in the organized sector is likely to increase from 21.5 lakh
tonnes to 33 lakh tonnes in case of 6% GDP growth and to 37.4
lakh tonnes in case of 8% GDP growth.
(d): Taking into account the above growth rate as well as
factors such as replacement costs, modernization and
improvements in the existing industry, etc., the total
investment in this sector has been estimated to increase from
Rs. 305 crores during the Ninth Plan to Rs. 1146 crores
during the Tenth Plan (at 2001 – 2002 prices) in case of GDP
growth of 6% and Rs. 1774 crores in case of GDP growth of 8%.

records.title: EXPENDITURE ON EDUCATION .
details:
(a) whether it is fact that the Education Commission had
recommended in 1964-65 that it was essential to spend 6 percent of
the total GDP annually on education;
(b) if so, whether such amount is still not being spent on
education, even after a lapse of nearly four decades; and
(c) if so, the reasons therefor and by when that much amount is
likely to be spent on Education in future?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
(PROF. RITA VERMA)
(a) to (c): The Kothari Commission on Education (1964-66) had
recommended that educational expenditure should rise from 2.9% in
1965-66 to 6% in 1985-86. However, the allocation and expenditure
on education has not so far reached this level due to competing
priorities and resource constraint. Constant and continuous
efforts are made to raise the allocation and expenditure on
education subject to overall availability of resources.

records.title: EXPLORATION OF OIL AND GAS .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that the work of production from the 
already-explored oil and natural gas reserves in our country has not been 
started so far;
(b) if so, what is the percentage of production being made from these 
reserves at present; and
(c) the reasons for not starting production from all these reserves so far?

MINISTER OF PETROLEUM & NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM NAIK)
(a) to (c): After the exploration phase, starting of production from any 
area depends on techno-commercial factors such as, the reservoir 
characteristics, the quality of hydrocarbons, the prices of oil and gas, the 
infrastructure availability and the logistics. There is also a lead time 
between a discovery during exploration phase and the production of 
hydrocarbons. The reserves from the areas where appraisal is under 
progress, or which are not viable for production at present, are not 
significant, around 5% or so.

(a)&(b): In order to develop the Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, the Government in 1995 established an independent Department of ISM&H in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. records.title: DUTIES ON INDIAN STEEL IMPORTS BY US .
details: to answer to Unstarred Question 2111, given in the Rajya Sabha on 7th December, 2001, and state how many times the rates of import duty on steel were increased by USA during the period from March, 1998 to February, 2002, and how much the same has been increased in each case alongwith the details of its effect on the steel trade of India?

MINISTER OF STATE (SHRI BRAJA KISHORE TRIPATHY)
OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL
 A statement is laid on the Table of the House.
 STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY OF THE RAJYA SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 395 TO BE ANSWERED ON 19/04/2002 TABLED BY S/SHRI KAPIL SIBAL AND RAJIV RANJAN SINGH `LALAN` REGARDING DUTIES ON INDIAN STEEL IMPORTS BY US
 The reply to Unstarred Question 2111 given in the Rajya Sabha on 7th December 2001 gives information on the anti dumping and countervailing anti subsidy duties imposed by the US against import of steel from India and not on the structure of import duty on steel existing in USA. The details of the anti dumping and countervailing investigations conducted by USA against import of steel items from India since April 99 are as given below:
(i) Cut-to-length Carbon Steel Plates: 
Nature of investigation Status/Details
Anti-dumping & Anti-Subsidy (Countervailing) US had initiated investigation in March, 1999. SAIL was the targeted company. Final duties (Anti-dumping 72.49%) (Anti-subsidy 12.8%) were imposed by US in February 2000. GOI has taken up the matter with the Dispute Settlement Body of WTO. A panel has been constituted to examine the issues in this dispute. First submission by GOI has been made before the Panel on 19th November, 2001. According to the schedule of the Panel, the final report would be circulated to WTO members by June, 2002.
(ii) Hot-rolled Steel Flat Products :
Nature of investigation Status/Details
Anti-dumping & Anti-subsidy (Countervailing) In December, 2000, the US DOC initiated these investigations. In November, 2001 US authorities have announced the final determination. The Anti-dumping duties (companywise) ranging from 36.53% to 44.40% and Anti-subsidy duties (companywise)ranging from 9.17% to 31.89% have been imposed in respect of the exports from India. 
(iii) Cold Rolled Steel Products : 
Nature of investigation Status/Details
Anti-dumping & Anti-Subsidy (Countervailing) In October 2001 the US ITC instituted AD/CVD investigations against import of certain cold-rolled steel products imported into USA from 20 countries including India. The preliminary determination was due on 7th March 2002. However in keeping with the petitioners request the US DOC has postponed the preliminary determination until 26.4.2002.
 In addition to the above the US President announced temporary safeguard measures on 5th March 2002 against import of certain steel products and imposing tariff of 8% to 30% and tariff rate quotas. India has been excluded from the safeguard action except in the category of carbon flanges for which the tafiff will be 13% (first year) 10% (second year) and 7% (third year).

details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

to part (a) above be in the negative, the reasons therefor and the present status of consideration?
ANSWER
MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R.BAALU)
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The approval is granted for a period of three years so as to facilitate re-consideration of the matter. 
(c) The broad parameters/conditionalities laid down interalia included:
(i) Every field where Bt cotton is planted shall be fully surrounded by a belt of land called `refuge` in which the same non-Bt cotton variety shall be sown. The size of the refuge belt should be such as to take at least five rows of non-Bt cotton or shall be 20% of total sown area whichever is more.
(ii) To facilitate this, each packet of seeds of the approved varieties should also contain a separate packet of the seeds of the same non-Bt cotton variety which is sufficient for planting in the refuge defined above. 
(iii) Each packet should be appropriately labeled indicating the contents and the description of the Bt hybrid including the name of the transgenes, the GEAC approval reference, physical and genetic purity of the seeds. The packet should also contain detailed directions for use including sowing pattern, pest management, suitability of agro-climatic conditions etc., in vernacular language. 
(iv) MAHYCO will enter into agreements with their dealers/agents, that will specify the requirements from dealers/agents to provide details about the sale of seeds, acreage cultivated, and State/Regions where Bt cotton is sown.
(v) MAHYCO will prepare annual reports by 31st March each year on the use of Bt cotton hybrid varieties by dealers, acreage, locality (State and Region) and submit the same in electronic form to GEAC, if asked for by the GEAC.
(d) Does not arise.

records.title: POLICY ON WATER SHARING
details:
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN SETHI) 
(a) to (e) The draft National Policy Guidelines for Water
Allocation amongst States were formulated by the National
Water Board in 1994 and were discussed by the Board during
its 6th and special meetings held on 17th March, 1994, 16th &
22nd June, 1994 respectively. The Guidelines enumerate
various concepts and definitions related to rivers, river
valleys and river basins, co-basins States, watersheds and
catchments, storage, withdrawal, consumptive use and
utilisation. The broad objective of the guidelines is to
optimally harness the inter-State river waters for the
betterment of the people of the co-basin States/Union
Territories to the extent such development are not
detrimental to the interests of other co-basin States.
General principles incorporated in the guidelines for
allocation of water are; equitable apportionment, allocation
amongst states vis-a-vis allocation amongst uses, right of
water use, inter-basin diversion, protection of existing
uses, existing inter-state agreements, parties to the process
of allocation, water quality, long distance water transfer 
(LDWT) etc. The Guidelines also enumerate various factors
for equitable distribution of water such as contribution of
each of the basin states in the water resources of the basin,
demand made by the states and its practicability for
utilisation, availability of alternative sources etc. It
also has provision for review of the allocation once made.
The draft guidelines were considered by National
Water Resources Council (NWRC) during its 3rd meeting held on
6th February, 1996. The States expressed divergent views on
these guidelines. The draft guidelines were reviewed by the
National Water Board in its 8th and 9th meetings held on 6th
November, 1996 and 19th November, 1997 respectively. After
detailed deliberations and certain modifications, a majority
of the members of the Board arrived at a broad consensus in
its 9th meeting. The draft guidelines so modified were
placed before NWRC in its 4th meeting held on 7th July, 2000
where no consensus could be arrived at. The National Water
Resources Council in its 5th meeting held on 1st April, 2002
has again referred the draft guidelines to the National Water
Board for having a re-look and arriving at a consensus on the
draft guidelines.

records.title: INCREASE IN COST OF AGRICULTURE PRODUCTION .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that the main problem of agriculture is the situation arising due to 
incessant increase in cost of production;
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto;
(c) whether it is also a fact that Indian Society of Agricultural Science and Indian Council 
of Agricultural Research have realized the need for comprehensive charges in research 
work, keeping in view the agriculture aspect of WTO; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof?

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV)
(a)&(b): No Sir. The cost of production of agricultural crops depends on cost of 
cultivation and productivity. Accordingly in case the productivity increases at a higher rate 
than the increase in cost of cultivation, the cost of production of such crops may actually 
decline. Conversely, the cost of production may increase. Thus seen over a period of time, 
the cost of production shows a fluctuating pattern.
(c)&(d): The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has been continuously 
pursuing the work of agricultural research and scientists are being apprised of the different 
agreements relating to agriculture in the WTO. ICAR has prepared its Draft 10th Five Year 
Plan keeping in view the WTO.

details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether Government have decided to reward the judges who will dispose of the
pending cases expeditiously;
(b) if so, the details of guidelines issued in this regard and when were

years or more in High Courts/Supreme Court and Supordinate Courts in a time-
bound manner;
(d) if so, the details threof; and
e) the new strategy likely to be envisaged to clear the pending cases 
in various courts?
ANSWER
MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFAIRS (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY)
(a) No, Sir.
(b) Question does not arise.
(c)to
(e): Hon`ble Chief Justice of India has addressed a letter dated the 
22nd April, 2002to theChief Justics of all High Courts to examine the matter
and consider the desirability of issuing necessary instructions to the 
Registry of the High Court as well as to the Courts subordinate to the High 
Court, to indentify and dispose of the matters which were more than 7 year
old as on 31st December, 1998. Further

the Minister of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs has by his lettr dated the 4th April, 2001 requested Chief 
Ministers of all States and Chief Justices of all High Courts to fill up 
the existing vacancies in subordinate jucidiary as one of the main reasons 
for delay in the disposal of cases in courts is the large number of vacant 
posts of judicial officers in the District/Subordinagte Courts. Moreover,
under article 235 of the Constitution of India, the administrative control 
over the members of subordinate judiciary vest with the concerned High Court.
Further, in exercise of powers conferred under proviso to article 309 read
with articles 233 and 234 of the Constitution, the concerned State Government
frames rules and regulations in consultation with the High Court exercising
jurisdiction in relation to each State. The members of the State Judicial 
Service are governed by these rules and regulations. The Delhi High Court 
has initiated `Unit Scheme` under which judicial officers will be assessed 
by according graded priority for disposal of old cases according to the year
of pendency.
Department-related Parliament Standing Committee on Home Affair, has since
given their Report on judicial reforms on 31st December, 2001. In their 
report, they have suggested various measures for speedy disposal of old 
pending cases. Their recommendations have been considered and the matter
has ben taken up with the State Governments/High Courts.

records.title: (clubbed) NEW TELECOM POLICY .
details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether Government had announced New Telecom Policy in 1999; 
(b) is so, the targets fixed for setting up of telephone network in the country under the policy: 
(c) whether telephone system has been expanded on the basis of said targets ; and 
(d) if so, the details with regard to achievement of the targets?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR)
(a) Yes, Sir.
(b) The targets fixed for setting up of telephone network in the country under the New Telecom Policy-1999 (NTP-99) are as follows:-
(i) Make available telephone on demand by the year 2002 and sustain it thereafter so as to achieve a teledensity of 7 by the year 2005 and 15 by the year 2010.
(ii) Encourage development of telecom in rural areas making it more affordable by suitable tariff structure and making rural communication mandatory for all fixed service providers.
(iii) Increase rural tele-density from the current level of 0.4 to 4 by the year 2010 and provide reliable transmission media in all rural areas.
(iv) Achieve telecom coverage of all villages in the country and provide reliable media to all exchanges by the year 2002.
(v) Provide Internet access to all district headquarters by the year 2000.
(vi) Provide high speed data and multimedia capability using technologies including Integrated Services Digital network (ISDN) to all towns with a population greater than 2 lac by the year 2002.
(c) & (d) Yes, Sir. The telephone system is being expanded by Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. (BSNL), Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (MTNL) and other licensed private operators to achieve the NTP-99 targets. The details are as follows:-
(i) 414.47 lakh Direct Exchange Lines (DELs) both (fixed and cellular) have been provided as on 31.01.2002.
(ii) Teledensity as on 31.01.2002 including fixed and mobile phones provided by BSNL, MTNL and other licensed Private Operators has reached 4.04 per 100 persons.
(iii) 4,29,515 villages out of the total of 6,07,491 villages have been provided with Village Public Telephones (VPTs) as on 31.01.2002.
(iv) 28,533 out of a total of 33,071 exchanges are already provided with reliable media as on 31.01.2002. The remaining exchanges are being covered progressively during the current year.
(v) Internet access is available to all District Headquarters.

records.title: ENFORCING QUOTA SYSTEM ON TEXTILE IMPORT .
details:
MINISTER OF STATE FOR TEXTILES 
(SHRI V. DHANANJAY KUMAR)
(a) to (c) Till December 31, 1994, the exports of textiles to certain developed countries (e.g. US; member countries of EU; Canada) had been governed by bilateral textile agreements entered into between India and these countries under the aegis of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement (MFA), outside the rules of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). With effect from January 1, 1995, the quantitative restrictions (import quotas) in the bilateral agreements under the MFA, are being governed by the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC) contained in the Final Act of the Uruguay Round negotiations of the GATT. Presently, our textiles and clothing items face restraints in USA, European Union and Canada. Quotas by themselves are trade restrictive. 
As per ATC, the textile quotas would be phased out and textile sector fully integrated into WTO by 1st January 2005. The Government has been raising the issues of meaningful integration including enhanced quota, under WTO Agreement on Textile and Clothing at various fora.

records.title: DEVALUATION OF RUPEE AGAINST U.S. DOLLAR
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that value of rupee has been 
decreasing constantly over the last few years in the country;
(b) if so, to what extent the value of Indian rupee has
 decreased against U.S. dollar from 
 March, 1998 to February 2002; and
(c) what has been its effects on India`s foreign trade?

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
( SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL )
(a) The exchange rate of the rupee against the US dollar, 
effective from March 1993, is largely market determined. 
Under this system, the rupee-dollar rate moves in both
directions on a day-to-day basis depending on the demand 
for and supply of foreign exchange in the market and 
short-term factors. The rupee-dollar rate is also influenced 
to some extent by the strength of the US dollar in the 
international currency markets.
(b) The rupee depreciated by 18.8 percent against the 
US dollar from the monthly average of Rs 39.50 per U.S.
dollar in March 1998 to the average of Rs. 48.66 in
February, 2002 (upto 21-2-2002). 
(c) The depreciation of rupee, given other things, is 
expected to help promote exports and strengthen our efforts
at cost-effective import substitution.

records.title: DELEGATION TO USA TO SEEK COOPERATION IN RESOLVING TERRORISM .
details:
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(CH. VIDYASAGAR RAO)
(a) & (b): Yes, Sir. Home Minister is expected to visit the United States at the invitation of the US Government as part of the process of strengthening India-US bilateral cooperation on counter-terrorism.
(c) & (d): India and the United States have an ongoing cooperation in combating terrorism through a Joint Working Group on Counter-terrorism. Besides sharing of information and assessment on terrorist groups in this region, the United States provides assistance through anti-terrorism training for law enforcement agencies in India, capacity building for consequence management and support for strengthening institutional structure in the country for combating terrorism. During the visit of Prime Minister to Washington from 7-9 November, 2001, the two sides agreed to launch a new initiative on cyber-terrorism. The two countries also coordinate efforts on counter-terrorism initiatives in the United Nations, including on a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism, sponsored by India.
 On 5th October, 2001 the White House spokesman had stated at a press briefing that President Bush had condemned the terrorist attack in Srinagar on 1st October, 2001 and that the President had also said that `Terrorism must end everywhere, and that includes in Kashmir`. Besides Harkat-ul-Mujahideen, which had been notified by the US State Department as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation, the US Department of Treasury has notified Jaish-e-Mohammad as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, along with Harkat-ul-Mujahideen and some other Pakistan-based organisations and individuals.

records.title: STRENGTHENING OF WATER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM .
details:
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SMT. BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) 
(a),(b) & (e) Flood is a natural phenomenon. Complete
protection to all flood affected areas against all
magnitudes of flood is neither practically feasible nor
economically viable. Reasonable protection against flood
using judicious combination of structural and non-
structural measures is the strategy adopted for flood
management. 
(c) & (d) Flood Management being a State subject, flood
control schemes are planned, funded and executed by the
State Governments themselves out of their own resources and
as per their own priorities. Central Government renders
assistance that are technical, catalytical and promotional
in nature.
The Government of India has set up Ganga Flood
Control Commission to tackle the flood problem in Ganga
basin, which has prepared comprehensive plans for flood
management for all the 23 river systems of Ganga basin.
Similarly, the Brahmaputra Board set up by the Government of
India under an Act of Parliament has prepared Master Plan
for main Brahmaputra and Barak Valley inter alia to control
floods in North Eastern region. These plans have been
forwarded to respective State
Governments for preparing detailed schemes based on ground
surveys and for implementation.
The Central Government has also set up 159 flood
forecasting Stations on major interstate rivers which give
timely warning to all flood affected regions in various
States.
The Government of India constituted several expert
committees to study the problem of floods in the country.
The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (RBA) set up in 1976 examined the
problem in detail and submitted its report in 1980. The
recommendations of RBA, which form the framework for flood
management strategy in the country, were forwarded to all
the state Governments for implementation.
Further, a number of other Expert Committees/Task
Forces were constituted from time to time to examine the
area/region specific problems relating to floods, whose
recommendations were also sent to the respective State
Governments for implementation.

records.title: EDIBLE OIL EXTRACTION INDUSTRY .
details: CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION

(a) whether it is a fact that the full use of installed capacity in edible oil extraction 
industry is possible by providing appropriate quantity of oilseeds;
(b) if so, Government`s reaction in this regard; and
(c) the total quantity of oilseeds production assessed to be required for using the full installed extraction capacity in the country?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
( SHRI V. SREENIVASA PRASAD )
(a)&(b): Yes, Sir. The domestic production of oilseeds is short of the total requirement
of Solvent Extraction Industry. In order to enhance utilization of capacity of the Solvent 
Extraction Industry, Government has allowed import of oilseeds and oil bearing materials except
coconut/copra under Open General License (OGL).
(c): There are 785 Solvent Extraction Plants having annual capacity of 337 lakhs MT in terms 
of oil bearing materials in the country. The requirement of the Solvent Extraction Industry for
full utilization of the installed capacity is, therefore, 337 lakhs MT in terms of oil bearing 
materials including oilseeds.

records.title: DECISION TAKEN BY NATIONAL WATER RESOURCES COUNCIL .
details:
(a) whether the meeting of National Water Resources Council was
 held in May, 2001;
(b) if so, the main issue undertaken for consideration and
decision in the meeting;
(c) whether any final decision was taken on this main issue after
consideration; and
(d) if so, the details of the decision?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SMT. BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY)
(a) to (d) The last 4th meeting of National Water Resources
Council was held on 7th July, 2000 under the chairmanship of the
Hon’ble Prime Minister of India. The deliberations established a
consensus among the States on most of the important issues
contained in the proposed draft updated National Water Policy and
proposed draft National Policy Guidelines for Water Allocation
amongst the States. However, some areas were found needing further
more discussions. In order to examine and for achieving greater
convergence and agreement on these issues as well, a Working Group
of Irrigation/Water Resources Ministers of all the States/Union
Territories under the Chairmanship of the Hon’ble Union Minister
of Water Resources was constituted on 9th October, 2000. The first
meeting of the Working Group was held on 22nd May, 2001 wherein
the draft updated National Water Policy was deliberated upon to
arrive at near consensus. The Working Group was unanimous on all
the provisions of the draft policy except provisions on “Setting
up of River Basin Organizations” and Water Allocation amongst
States.” A Core Group under the Chairmanship of Union Minister of
State for Water Resources with the Irrigation/Water Resources
Ministers from Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Goa, Karnataka, Punjab,
Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu as its members was constituted to arrive
at a consensus on the above two provisions of the draft updated
National Water Policy. The Core Group has submitted its report
which would be discussed in the next meeting of the Working
Group. After finalisation of the draft policy by the Working
Group, the same would be considered by the National Water
Resources Council for its approval.

details:
MINISTER OF STATE (INDEPENDENT CHARGE) OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRIES OF PLANNING, STATISTICS & PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE)
(a) and (b) The Chairman of the Disinvestment Commission demitted his office at the end of his tenure on 30.11.1999. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The Commission has been reconstituted on 24th July, 2001. 
(d) The names of the other members of the Commission are in the process of finalisation. 
(e) The criteria for appointment of the members of the Commission are that persons of eminence and expertise from sectors such as finance, industry, management, economics are given representation.
(f) The terms of reference of the Commission are as under:
(i) It shall be an advisory body and its role and function would be to advise the Government on Disinvestment in those public sector units that are referred to it by the Government.
(ii) It shall also advise the Government on any other matter relating to disinvestment as may specifically be referred to it by the Government, and also carry out any such other activities relating to disinvestment as may be assigned to it by the Government.
(iii) In making its recommendations, it will also take into consideration the interest of workers, employees and other stakeholders, in the public sector units(s).
(iv) The final decision on the recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission will vest with the Government.

records.title: LAND COVERED BY ANY CATCHMENT AREAS .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a certain part of land in
 the country which does not fall under any catchment area;
(b) if so, total area of such land and the percentage of this
land out of the total land;
(c) whether Government have made assessment of the requirement
of water for such land; and
(d) if so, the extent of water required for such land?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SMT. BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) 
(a) to (d) The geographical area of the country has been divided
into 20 river basins. Area North of Ladakh, not draining into
Indus, and areas of Andaman, Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands do
not fall in any of these basins. These areas constitute 36,758
square kilometer which is 1.12% of the total geographical area
of the country. Requirement of water is closely related to
population, demand for food, production of industrial items,
production of energy and preserving ecology. The area of North
Ladakh remains snow-bound round the year and is largely
uninhabited having negligible water requirement. The requirement
of water for Andaman, Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands is of the
order of 950 million cubic meter which is met by harnessing the
abundant rainfall in these areas.

records.title: RISE AND DECLINE IN PRODUCTION OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that production of agricultural products came down during 2000-
2001, in comparison to 1999-2000;
(b) if so, the details of agricultural products and the estimated decline in production of 
each of them;
(c) the details of agricultural products whose production increased in 2000-2001, in 
comparison to 1999-2000; and
(d) the extent of such increase and the reasons behind the decrease and increase, 
respectively, in case of the said agricultural products?

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD Y. NAIK)
(a)to(d): According to advance estimates of production for 2000-01, the production of 
foodgrains, total oilseeds and commercial crops such as cotton is expected to be lower than 
that of the final estimates for 1999-2000. However, it is likely to be higher in case of certain 
crops such as bajra, maize, barley, other kharif pulses, groundnut and sugarcane during 
2000-01 compared to the preceding year. The crop-wise details of expected 
decrease/increase are annexed.
 The year 2000-01 experienced adverse weather conditions. The overall rainfall 
during monsoon 2000 was deficient by 8% and this deficiency accentuated during the 
subsequent seasons. Deficient rains adversely affected the irrigation potential also. Since 
only 38.4% of net area sown is irrigated, these weather aberrations adversely affected 
agriculture production and productivity and hence there is lower production of those crops 
which require more water, There is marginal increase in production of certain coarse 
cereals, other kharif pulses, and groundnut as they can better withstand moisture stress.

records.title: TALKS BETWEEN INDIA AND PAKISTAN .
details:
(a)
whether it is a fact that a number of round of talks have been held between India and Pakistan over the years; and
(b)
if so, when, where and at which levels the same were held and what have been the main issues during each round of talks?

THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH)
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) India is committed to establishing peaceful, friendly and cooperative relations with Pakistan. While working towards this objective, over the last three years (July 1997-July 2001) the following have been the significant bilateral meetings between India and Pakistan:
(i) In 1998, India initiated the Composite Dialogue involving bilateral discussions at the official level on 8 identified subjects. The Composite Dialogue seeks to build trust and confidence, establish a stable structure of cooperation and address outstanding issues between the two countries. Discussions on Peace & Security including CBMs (Foreign Secretary level), and Jammu & Kashmir (Foreign Secretary level) were held at Islamabad from 16 to 18 October 1998. Discussions on Siachen (Defence Secretary), Sir Creek (Surveyor General/Additional Secretary), Tulbul (Secretaries Water & Power), Terrorism and Drug Trafficking (Home/Interior Secretaries), Economic and Commercial Cooperation(Commerce Secretaries), and Friendly Exchanges (Secretaries, Culture) were held at New Delhi from 5 to 13 November 1998.
(ii) In February 1999, Prime Minister Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited Lahore on the inaugural Delhi-Lahore bus service. During the visit the Lahore Declaration was signed by the Prime Ministers of India and Pakistan, a Memorandum of Understanding was signed by the Foreign Secretaries of both countries, and both sides issued a Joint Statement. 
(iii) In March 1999, External Affairs Minister, Shri Jaswant Singh met his Pakistani counterpart at Nuwara Eliya, Sri Lanka on the margins of the SAARC Council of Ministers meeting and discussed matters pertaining to follow-up of the Prime Minister`s Lahore visit held earlier in the year. The Foreign Secretaries also met. 
(iv) In July 2001, President Pervez Musharraf visited India on an invitation from Prime Minister Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee. The Summit level meeting contributed to a better understanding of each sides view point. The entire gamut of our relations were discussed during these talks. India emphasised the need to build an atmosphere of trust for progress on all outstanding issues including Jammu & Kashmir. We also focussed on cross border terrorism and conveyed that India had the resolve, strength and stamina to counter terrorism and violence till it was decisively crushed. 
 In addition to the above meetings, in June 1999, External Affairs Minister Shri Jaswant Singh met his Pakistani counterpart Mr. Sartaj Aziz at New Delhi, during the Kargil conflict. During this meeting Pakistan was told in clear terms that Pakistan`s armed intrusion and aggression at Kargil has to be vacated.

records.title: POWER GENERATION THROUGH CAPTIVE POWER PROJECTS .
details:
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER
( SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA )
(a): Yes, Sir.
(b): Details regarding the total installed capacity and the quantity of power being 
generated by captive power plants are not available as under Section 44 of the Electricity 
(Supply) Act, 1948, the State Electricity Boards give consent to setting up of captive 
power plants by various industries. However, as per information available with the 
Central Electricity Authority, as on March 31, 1999, 20 selected industries (having an 
installed capacity of 1 MW and above) have set up a captive generating capacity of 
13,932 MW in the country which generated 48354 GwHr of power. Details are given in 
the Annexure. 
(c) & (d): On July 11, 2001 the Ministry of Power has circulated a Captive Power 
Policy prepared by the Ministry of Power in consultation with the CEA to all the State 
Governments and Union Territories. In this policy, the following has been reiterated:
 If captive plant is of Hydro or cogeneration, such plant, irrespective of its size, 
may be permitted liberally.
 If captive power plant is based on coal or liquid fuel or gas such plant may be 
allowed and capacity of the plant permitted up to 200% of the requirement of 
industry (If the State is deficit in power).
 Captive power plant may be allowed if State/SEB or successor entity are unable 
to supply the required power supply. Such a captive power plant can be 
considered for the uninterrupted power supply to the industry even if the State is 
surplus in power.
 If the industry requires quality power supply which is not available, the proposal 
for installation of the captive power plant can be considered.
 If the cost of generation from captive power plant is found to be lower, the 
proposal may be considered after examining the cost and tariff.
 Units in Special Economic Zone (SEZs) and/industrial entities may be allowed to 
set up captive power plants liberally.
 Banking facilities are proposed to be provided to CPPs. The rates for banking may 
be determined on mutually agreed terms.
 Prior approval of SEB has to be obtained for wheeling of power. Wheeling will 
be done to any service (HT or LT). Wheeling charges may be worked out based 
on pooled rates worked out by Central/State Transmission Utility of that region.
 The tariff for sale of power from thermal CPPs, may be fixed after mutual 
discussion and could be based on pooled variable charge of thermal power 
stations operating in the SEB plus some percentage of the pooled variable charges 
as incentive. Tariff could also be based on the highest variable cost in the system 
or actual variable cost of CPP, whichever is lower and some percentage of the 
variable cost as an incentive.
 Third party sale is also permissible with the approval of SEB.

records.title: INDIGENOUS PRODUCTION OF CRUDE OIL .
details:
Minister of State in the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas (Shri Santosh Kumar Gangwar)
(a) to (c): A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.
Statement referred to in reply to parts (a) to (c) of Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No.1079 to be answered on 31.7.2001 regarding indigenous production of crude oil
(a) & (b): Yes, Sir. Several important steps have been taken to increase crude oil production in the country, which include : 
(i) To improve the recovery factor from existing major fields by implementing Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)/Improved Oil Recovery (IOR) schemes; in particular Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) has taken up 15 fields for this purpose at an estimated investment of Rs. 10,000 crore, which would also help in accelerating oil production from these fields. 
(ii) To increase exploration efforts through the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP). Under the first round of NELP, Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) have been signed for 24 blocks in which works are in progress. Additionally, another 25 blocks have been offered under the second round of NELP, of which PSCs have been signed on17.7.2001 for 23 blocks. 
(iii) To attract technology and investment; PSCs for 9 discovered fields, 8 in Gujarat and 1 in Assam, were signed on 23.2.2001 with consortia of Indian and foreign companies. 
(iv) To explore in new areas, especially in deep water and difficult frontier areas, as also explore in the deeper layers of the producing fields. 
(v) To develop faster the newly discovered fields and to step up the use of new technologies for seismic surveys, work over, stimulation operations, drilling of wells etc. in producing areas.
 In any field, generally a combination of various efforts are implemented simultaneously and thus it is difficult to attribute oil gain to any individual effort. The Enhanced Oil Recovery/Improved Oil Recovery schemes are long term measures, the implementation of which takes about 4 to 5 years and the gain therefrom is spread over the next twenty years or so. However, with various efforts undertaken the declining trend of crude oil production has been arrested with more production in 2000-01 as compared to the previous year.

records.title: WITHDRAWAL OF CEASEFIRE IN JAMMU AND KASHMIR AND ITS EXTENSION IN NORTH EASTERN STATES .
details:
(a) whether Government have withdrawn the cease-fire in Jammu and Kashmir State while the time period and the area of cease-fire in North-Eastern States have been extended; and
(b) if so, the comprehensive details thereof and reasons therefor ?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
( CH. VIDYASAGAR RAO )
(a) & (b): The Peace Initiative comprising restrictions on security forces initiating combat operations against terrorists in Jammu & Kashmir was announced by Government keeping in view the longing for peace and normalcy amongst the people of J&K and with the hope that terrorist outfits will appreciate this and all violence in the State and infiltration across the Line of Control and the International Border will cease and an atmosphere conducive for holding dialogue would be created. However terrorist groups have not recognised the imperatives of peace, dialogue and cooperation and have not shunned violence thereby hindering the peace process and inflicting misery upon the people. In view of this the cease-fire was not extended further beyond May 31st 2001.
 In North Eastern States, Government has entered into cease-fire with NSCN(K) for a period of one year with effect from 28th April, 2001. The cease-fire is valid in the State of Nagaland. Cease-fire with NSCN(I/M) which is in currency since 1.8.1997 has been further extended for a period of one year with effect from 1st August, 2001. The extension of cease-fire is without territorial limits. However the extension of area is being reviewed Government is committed to holding talks to restoration of peace with all those militant groups who give up the path of violence.

nominal fee.

records.title: ASSESSMENT OF IMPACT ON IT .
details:
-

information technology industry of India after USA`s proposal to make
 deduction in the information technology; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the assessment of impact on the information technology industry as a result thereof?

MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN) (a),(b) and (c): The Government has been in close touch
with the IT Software Industry Associations, prominent Indian Software 
Companies, the Embassy of India in the US and leading experts in the field to 
make an assessment of the impact of the slow down in the US economy on the
Information Technology Industry. While there is general agreement that the
slow down in the US economy is having an adverse impact on the Indian 
Software Industry, there are different opinions about the extent of the decline 
in business and the duration for which this decline will continue. 
The principal impact being faced by the Indian Software Sector is 
increased pressure on margins. A solution for dealing with the 
situation that has found favour with industry is making pro- 
active efforts to develop and exploit markets in countries 
such as Germany, France, Italy, Australia, Japan etc. The 
Ministry of Information Technology has cooperation agreement 
with these countries which provide for exploring opportunities 
to develop bilateral trade and efforts have been mounted to 
enable Indian Companies to explore these markets more fully.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER
( SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA )
(a) & (b) : Dabhol Power Company has served notices of conciliation and arbitration 
as per the provisions of the counter guarantee issued by the Government of India, on

(c) & (d) : As per the Government of India (GOI) counter guarantee issued to the 
Dabhol power project on 15.9.1994, arbitration proceedings, if any, arising out of dispute,

the `Settlement of Disputes` provides as follows :-
 Any dispute or difference (each a `dispute`) arising out of or in connection with 
this Guarantee shall, regardless of the nature of the dispute, be referred to the dispute 
resolution procedure in this section.
(A) The parties shall first seek an amicable settlement of the disputes by conciliation.
(i) Such conciliation shall take place in accordance with UNCITRAL Conciliation 
Rules (the `Conciliation Rules`) as at present in force and shall be conducted by three 
conciliators (or such lesser number as the parties may agree) to be appointed according 
to the Conciliation Rules.
(ii) Any meetings with the conciliators shall be held at New Delhi, India.
(iii) Each of the parties hereby gives for the purpose of the conciliation, undertakings 
and assurances as contained in the Conciliation Rules including an undertaking to 
promptly deposit its share of advance for payment of the costs as estimated by the 
conciliators.
(B) Any dispute that remains unresolved in accordance with the procedure outlined 
above in sub-paragraph 13(a), within sixty days or within such period as may be 
extended by the parties with mutual consent, shall be resolved by arbitration.
(i) Such arbitration shall be in accordance with the provisions of the UNCITRAL 
Arbitration Rules (the `Arbitration Rules`) as at present in force and shall be conducted 
by three arbitrators to be appointed according to the Arbitration Rules.
(ii) The arbitration proceedings shall be held in London, England.
(iii) the third arbitrator appointed pursuant to this paragraph shall not be a national 
of India or of the United States.
(iv) The language of any conciliation and/or arbitration proceedings shall be English.
(v) Amounts due under any arbitration award shall be paid within 30 (thirty) days of 
the award and interest shall accrue thereafter on unpaid amounts under the award at the 
rate referred to in paragraph 1 (of the counter guarantee).
(vi) Notwithstanding any other provision of this Guarantee, the law governing this 
arbitration agreement shall be the law of the place where the arbitration proceedings are 
held.
(vii) Any award given pursuant to arbitration in London, England, under clause 
(ii) 
shall be governed by the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of 
Foreign Arbitral Awards of 1958.
(viii) If at any time, there are arbitration awards in favour of the Company under each 
of this Guarantee and the Government of Maharashtra (GOM) Guarantee which remain 
unpaid, then any proceedings in India for enforcement, attachment or execution which 
the Company may initiate with respect to the award under this Guarantee shall be 
initiated not earlier than 30 (thirty) days after enforcement, attachment or execution is

records.title: LOSSES SUFFERED BY BANKS DUE TO RECESSION IN SHARE MARKETS
details:
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL) 
(a)&(b) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued detailed guidelines to all commercial banks on banks investments in shares and financing of equities. These guidelines, inter-alia, stipulate that subjec to the overall exposure to sensitive sectors, a bank`s exposure to capital market by way of invesmens in shares, debentures and units of mutual funds (other than debt funds) through primary orsecondary markets should not exceed 5% of its total outstandings domestic credit as on 31st Marchof the previous year. These guidelines also stipulate that, as a prudential measure, banks` investment in equities etc. should not normally exceed 20% of its net worth.
RBI has reported that the total exposure of the Banking System by way of investment in the capital market, as on 31st January, 2001, stood at Rs. 8770.55 crore, which formed1.97%ofthebanks` ousandings advances. RBI has further reported that the banks also lend against the securities like shares debentures etc. and the total exposure of the banks in this category was less than 2% of their advances. According to RBI, although the exact loss incurred by banks is not readily available, it is no expeced to be large. 
(c)&(d): RBI has reported that the loss in investment and lending operations arise mainly on account of fall in the market value of the securities, for which margins are usually kept. The banks also take the personal guarantee of the borrowers to cover losses on account of fall in the value of securities. However, banks have their own internal guidelines to ensure prevention of irregularities/frauds and fix saff accountability.
