 ANNEX -II
Handloom Sector: 
(i) Workshed-cum-housing Scheme for Handloom Weavers: This is a production-cum-welfare oriented scheme and it was introduced in 1985-86 with the objective of providing a dwelling unit and a suitable workplace to weavers to improve their productivity and earnings. The scheme is being implemented by the respective State Handloom Corporations, primary societies or other specialized agencies nominated by the Government 
(ii) Project Package Scheme (PPS) for Handloom Weavers: The PPS aims to provide infrastructural support for increasing production, productivity and marketing of handloom products, protect traditional ethnic and languishing crafts and adopt an area development approach for development of handlooms in hilly and sparsely populated areas. The scheme is being funded on the basis of equal sharing of contribution by Central and State Government/implementing agency. 
(iii) Handloom Development Centres and Quality Dyeing Units: The aim of setting up of HDCs and QDUs is to make necessary arrnagements for procurement of hank yarn, preparing production plans keeping in view the market demand and set up marketing outlets. 
(iv) Group Insurance Scheme: The Group Insurance Scheme was introduced in 1992-93 in order to meet socio-economic obligation of weavers towards their family and the uncertainty of their working capacity, particularly in old age. Under the scheme a weaver is provided with insurance coverage of Rs. 10,000 for an annual premium of Rs.120. The premium is shared equally among the beneficiary, Central Government and the State Government. 
(v) New Insurance Scheme: A new insurance package scheme for handloom weavers was introduced in 1997-98. The new scheme provides for enhanced coverage against various types of risks at the same premium of Rs. 120. However, the share of the Central Government has been increased from Rs. 40 to Rs. 60 per annum and the share of weavers has been reduced from Rs. 40 to Rs. 20 per annum. 
(vi) Health Package Scheme : The Health Package Scheme was introduced in 1992-93 with the objective of ameliorating some of the health problems related to the profession of handloom weaving. Under the scheme the weavers are provided financial assistance for treatment of diseases like asthama, TB, etc. and for meeting the cost of testing of eyes and spectacles, supply of drinking water, maternity problems. 
(vii) Thrift Fund Scheme: The Thrift Fund Scheme was introduced in 1985-86 as a welfare scheme for handloom weavers and it was modified in the year 1991-92. The scheme aims at creation of a fund in the nature of provident fund with 8% of wages earned as contribution from the weaver and 4% of the wages each from Central Government and the State Governments. The fund earns saving bank interest rate. 
(viii) Market Development Assistance: The Market Development Assistance Scheme provides marketing assistance to the handloom sector. This is in lieu of Share Capital Assistance Scheme to Apex Societies and Corporations, Share capital and managerial subsidy to Primary Societies and Special Rebate Scheme. Apart from providing assistance to State Handloom Weavers Cooperative Societies, it also envisages providing assistance to national level handloom organisations viz. All India Handloom Fabrics Marketing Cooperative Societies Ltd., Delhi; North Eastern handicrafts and Handloom Development Corporation, Guwahati; Rehabilitation Industries Corporation, New Delhi, etc. The MDA assistance to the state organisation is shared equally by the respective State Governments and Central Government. 
(ix) Janata Cloth Scheme: This scheme was launched in 1976 and continued after 1993 till 1997-98 with modifications. The aim of the revised scheme (1993) was (1) to provide sustained income to handloom weavers particularly, the semi-skilled weavers by partially off-setting the cost disadvantage of handloom sector; (2) to enable handloom weavers graduate to production of higher value textile goods so as to earn higher wages; and (3) to provide alternate employment to handloom weavers displaced on account of phasing out of Janata Cloth Scheme. 
(x) Mill Gate Price Scheme: The Mill Gate Price Scheme is operated through National Handloom Development Corporation (NHDC) and is meant for supply of hank yarn to handloom weavers at mill gate prices.In order to help marketing of handloom textiles by various agencies and to make available handloom items under one roof in various townships having potential for marketing of handloom items, the concept of group merchandizing in the form of marketing complexes has been designed and National Handloom Development Corporation has been entrusted with the task of implementation of the concept. 
(xi) Development of Exportable Products and their Marketing: In order to give substantial impetus to the export of handloom fabric, made-ups and other handloom items from the country, Scheme for Development of Exportable Products and their marketing has been introduced during 1996-97. Under the Scheme, assistance is available for developing exportable products, for building up of production capability for export and thereafter marketing it.
 The project cost in respect of the agencies sponsored by the State Government is shared by the State Government itself or by the beneficiary agency. The agencies sponsored by Central Government are entitled to 100% assistance from the Government of India under the Scheme. 
(xii) Publicity and Exhibition: To provide marketing support to handloom agencies and the individual weavers, the office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms organizes the National Handloom Expos, District Level Events, Craft Melas, etc. in different parts of the country. For this purpose, the financial support is provided to the implementing agency towards infrastructure, publicity, etc. These activities are supportive to the handloom agencies, weavers and also to the consumer as it provides them an opportunity to purchase the handloom products of various states under one roof. 
Powerloom Sector: 
(a) Powerloom Service Centre(PSC): Under this scheme Powerloom Service Centres have been established at important locations. These Centres are responsible not only for imparting training to powerloom weavers but also for creating new designs and providing testing facilities. Till date 43 PSCs have been set up. 
(b) Powerloom Workers` Insurance Scheme: The Government of India introduced a Group Insurance Scheme for Powerloom workers in association with the Life Insurance Corporation of India during the year 1992-93. All Powerloom workers of age between 18 and 60 years and those who work during the year are eligible for insurance under this Scheme. A weaver, who had earned at least minimum average pay of Rs. 700 per month during a year, can join the Scheme. The Scheme envisages an annual premium to be shared equally by the Central Government, the State Government and the Powerloom worker. 
(c) Computer Aided Design Centres: For providing facilities for design development and product diversification for the powerloom sector, Computer Aided Design Centres are being set up at important powerloom centres.
Research & Development
The Government has taken up a programme for providing facilities to meet the testing needs of the country. Under this programme existing laboratories are being upgraded and wherever required new laboratories are being established. The prime objective is to provide testing facilities at easy distance to the textile industry.

(a),(b),(c)&(d) Despite the set-backs to ISI`s activities in J&K, Punjab and other parts of the country, there is no let up in its efforts to destabilize the country.
 Government is aware of the sinister designs of the ISI and has taken all necessary measures to curb its evil designs. It has been regularly sharing he inputs and sensitizing the concerned state Government and agencies regarding the activities of ISI. In order to prevent infiltration, border fencing and flood lighting has been undertaken along stretches of the Indo-Pakistan and Indo-Bangladesh border, besides strengthening the border management in general, including deployment of Units of Para Military Forces and Army. records.title: . POWER PRODUCTION IN THE HYDRO ELECTRIC SECTOR
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to 
 promote the production of power in hydro-electric sector;
(b) if not, the reasons therefor;
(c) whether Government have found out the possibilities of 
 utilization of capacity of power production in the 
 hydro-electric sector in northern, eastern, western and southern 
 regions of the country; and
(d) if so, the total amount of un-utilised power production 
 capacity in each region and what are the schemes to utilize 
 the same?

THE MINISTER OF POWER ( SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM )
(a) to (d) : A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.
STATEMENT
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (d) OF STARRED 
QUESTION NO. 246 TO BE ANSWERED IN THE RAJYA SABHA ON 15.12.1999 
REGARDING POWER PRODUCTION IN THE HYDRO-ELECTRIC SECTOR.
(a) & (b) : Yes, Sir. The Government had announced a policy 
on hydro power development in August, 1998 with the objective of 
accelerating the pace of hydro power development in the country. 
The share of hydro power has been continuously declining during 
the last three decades. As against an ideal hydel - thermal mix 
of 40:60, the share has gone down from 44% in 1970s to 25% in 
1999. An improvement in the hydel thermal mix is proposed to be 
achieved by 
(i) completion of the on-going hydroelectric 
projects; 
(ii) initiating advance action for obtaining necessary 
approvals in respect of new hydroelectric projects for which DPR 
is available; and 
(iii) initiating work on survey and 
investigation in respect of new green field sites to enable 
preparation of DPR so that necessary approvals could be obtained 
and projects taken up for execution in a phased manner.
(c) & (d) : The Central Electricity Authority on the basis of 
assessment carried out during 1978-87 had assessed the 
economically exploitable hydro potential of the country at 84,044 
MW at 60% load factor. The region-wise position as on 1.12.1999 
with regard to assessed potential, potential developed and under 
development is indicated in Annexure-I.
There is a substantial scope for promoting 
hydroelectric projects in North Eastern and Northern regions. A 
list of hydroelectric projects under execution is at Annexure-II. 
The region-wise list of hydroelectric projects in the Central 
Sector which are proposed to be taken up for benefits during the 
10th Plan is at Annexure-III. The region-wise list of projects to 
be taken up in the Central Sector in respect of which survey and 
investigations are proposed to be taken up in order to enable 
preparation of DPRs is at Annexure-IV.
In the Southern region, efforts are being made in 
consultation with the Governments of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to 
promote hydroelectric projects in the Cauvery basin which could 
not be taken up due to inter-state river dispute.
(Annexure will get later on or scan from file )

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (c),(d),(e) & 
(f) OF RAJYA SABHA UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 949 FOR ANSWER
ON 9TH DECEMBER, 1999.
The Government has been taking measures from time to time to
improve and re-organise its administrative set up to promote
efficiency, keeping in view the needs of changing environment. The
steps taken in the recent past include the following:
(i) Several Ministries/Departments/Organisations with considerable
public interface have introduced Citizens` Charters indicating
broadly the quality of service, the public would be entitled
to, within a specified time frame. Information and
Facilitation Counters have been set up by 45
Ministries/Departments/Central Government Organisations to
provide information on procedures and the schemes of the
concerned organisation as well as to access information
pertaining to the status of individual cases.
(ii) Steps have also been taken to strengthen the existing machinery
for redress of public grievances. Most of the
Ministries/Departments have fixed time limits for handling
grievances received from the Members of Parliament, and the
names of the officers handling grievances have been publicised.
A system of categorising all the grievances and their
computerised monitoring has been installed in various
Ministries/Departments and this is linked to the main terminal
in the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public
Grievances.
(iii) The Government has also taken up simplification of laws, rules
and procedures for improving efficiency in the organisations.
Towards this end, over 40 Departments have undertaken, through
expert Task Forces or by internal exercises, a detailed review
of laws, regulations and procedures administered by them.
(iv) A Commission on Review of Administrative Laws was set up on 8
May, 1998 under the Chairmanship of Shri P.C. Jain with a view
to identify proposals for amendment/repeal of existing laws,
regulations and procedures having inter-sectoral impact so as
to make them objective, transparent and predictable. The
Commission submitted its report on 30 September, 1998. The
important recommendations of the Commission include repeal of
almost 50% of Central Laws (1382 out of 2500 Laws), expeditious
amendments to a critical list of 109 identified Acts,
documentation of administrative laws (rules, regulations,
executive instructions) by all the Ministries/Departments,
harmonisation of statutes and laws with reference to the
perspective of domestic and foreign investors, trade and
industry, consumers, exporters and importers, and development
of a viable alternative disputes resolution machinery. The
Government has constituted a Standing Committee under the
Chairmanship of Secretary(Personnel) for monitoring the
follow-up action on implementation of the recommendations
contained in the report. The Committee has held fifteen
meetings with different Ministries/Departments in groups. Most
of the Ministries/Departments have initiated action to make
suitable amendments/modifications to or repeal the Acts and
Laws being administered by them with a view to improve service
delivery and bring about transparency in the functioning of
Government.

records.title: BAN ON EXPORT OF MEAT FRUITS AND VEGETABLES H
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that Law Commission has recommended to ban the 
export of meat, fruits and vegetables due to shortage and excessive 
price hike in the country;
(b) if so, whether the Commission has also advised to amend the 
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development 
Authority Act; and
(c) whether Government have considered this and if so, the decision 
thereon?

MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI MARAN)
a) Yes, Sir.
b) No, Sir. The Law Commission has only recommended that it would 
be appropriate that the Government issues a notification prohibiting 
the export of vegetables, meat (excluding beef) and fruits altogether 
with a view to ensure their availability to the poorer sections of the 
society at reasonable rates.
c) The Government has examined the recommendation made by the Law 
Commission. Keeping in view the demand and supply position, 
growers’ interest and India’s long-term export interest in meat, fruits 
and vegetables, it is not the opportune time to ban the export of these 
items.

records.title: PRODUCTION OF PULSES
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that in a country of vegetarian people, pulses 
not only constitute a part of their normal meal but these are nutritious also 
and their production in the country is less than their requirement; 
(b) if so, what has been the total production of pulses in the country 
during the years 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99, separately; 
(c) what has been the year-wise estimated rate of production, per hectare,
of pulses during the above years in the country; and 
(d) the extent to which the above rate is lower as compared to pulse 
exporting countries of the world? 
 A N S W E R

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE
 (SHRI SBPBK SATYANARAYANA RAO)
(a): Pulses are one of the major sources of protein. The per capita requirement of protein per day is assessed by Indian Council of Medical
Research (ICMR) at 60 gms for man and 50 gms for woman out of which
contribution of pulses is about two-thirds i.e. 33 gms. per day. 65% of the 
weight of pulses contain protein. Thus to obtain 33 gms per capita per day of 
proteins, 53 gms pulses are required per capita per day. At this rate the 
annual requirement works out to about 180 lakh Metric tonnes. As against 
this, the availabliity is 158.9 lakh Metric tonnes.
(b): The total production of pulses in the country during the years 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99 is given below:-

records.title: SIMPLIFICATION OF PROCEDURE FOR FOREIGN CAPITAL INVESTMENT
details:
Minister of State in the Ministry of Finance
 ( Balasaheb Vikhe Patil )
 (a) & (b) : In furtherance of the ongoing liberalisation efforts, Government has taken initiatives to boost inflow of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) like conveying decision on all FIPB proposals within 30days, allowing 100% foreign equity in construction & maintenance of roads, highways, vehicular tunnels, ports & Harbour subject to certain minimum conditions. Prior approval of RBI for FDI proposals under the automatic as well as FIPB route have been dispensed with.
 Foreign Investment Implementation Authority has been constituted which overseas the implementation of FIPB approvals.
 Certain initiatives to attract portfolio investments from FIIs have recently been taken which include simplification in registration requirements of sub-accounts and permissions for tendering securities directly in terms of takeovers, for trading in derivative contracts and for hedging foreign exchange risk through purchase of forward cover on incremental equity investments. The 100% Debt Fund FIIs have been permitted to invest in unlisted debt securities in addition to listed debt securities.
 Certain policy initiatives have also been taken with a view to simplify procedure for NRI investment in mutual funds, extending screen-based automated trading overseas, revising portfolio investment ceiling for NRIs/PIOs/OCBs from 1% to 5% and 5% to 10% respectively, simplifying procedure for extension of validity for NRIs/PIOs/OCBs and introduction of one stage approval for all schemes following under RBI approval mechanism.
 Guidelines on Euro Issues have been relaxed permitting unlisted company for floating issues, removal of stipulation of validity period and permitting Information Technology Service companies to issue ADR/GDR linked stock option to their employees.
 (c ) & (d) : Certain sectors like Arms and ammunition and allied items, Defence equipment, Atomic Energy, Real Estate, Housing, Agriculture and Plantation etc. are not open for Foreign Direct Investment.

records.title: AREAS AFFECTED BY RECENT EARTHQUAKE IN CHAMOLI .
details:
MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI)
(a&b): Yes Sir. An earthquake of magnitude 6.8 on Richter scale occurred on 
29.3.1999 at 00 hrs 35 min. 1ST in Chamoli District of Uttar Pradesh. The six 
districts viz. Chamoli, Rudraprayag, Tehri Garhwal, Bageshwar, Uttar Kashi and 
Pauri Garhwal were affected by the earthquake. 
(c): The impact of the earthquake was comparatively more severe in the districts 
of Chamoli and Rudraprayag. The survey conducted so far by GSI in the Garhwal 
Himalayas has shown that damage in the form of large cracks, failure of 
individual structural elements, collapse of partition walls, particularly those 
made of mud mortar, has been observed in an approximate area of 1800 sq. km 
spread in Chamoli, Rudraprayag and Tehri districts. The reinforced concrete 
structures have suffered minor damages only. The estimated intensity in this 
area is VII on MSK scale.
The maximum intensity noted in the narrow epicentral tract including Chamoli is 
VIII. Studies are continuing to constrain various isoseismal zones in the area 
being surveyed.

records.title: ROLE OF UNO IN REGARD OF NATO S ATTACKS .
details:
(a) Whether it is a fact that the U.N. Security Council was not able to play a 
satisfactory role in peace keeping at the recent attacks on Yugoslavia by the 
NATO countries;
(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard;
(c) Whether Government have considered the necessity of bringing comprehensive 
improvement in the present structure and working of the U.N.O.; and
(d) if so, the action taken in this regard ?

THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH)
a. The UN Security Council had been considering the developments in & b. the 
autonomous province of Kosovo, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It had authorised 
the Contact Group on the former Yugoslavia to deal with the situation in Kosovo. 
However, without due authorisation of the Council, NATO launched attacks against 
the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Government has been closely following these 
developments and expressed its serious concern on March 24 and 25, 1999. Our 
statements have categorically expressed themselves against any action unilateral 
or otherwise, in contravention of the UN Charter. This unilateral action has 
seriously undermined the authority of the entire UN system. We have called for 
the resolution of crisis through peaceful means within the framework of the 
sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.
C & d: India supports expansion of the UN Security Council with a view to 
enhance representation of developing countries in permanent as well as 
non-permanent members` category. Expansion and reform should be integral parts 
of a common package. India is taking active part in the discussions of the 
Open-Ended Working Group of the UN General Assembly on Security Council 
restructuring.

records.title: CONTAINING DMS EXPENDITURE .
details:
(a) whether any action has been taken by Government to contain the continuous 
losses to the Delhi Milk Scheme; 
(b) if so, whether possibilities have been explored to have a cut on various 
existing items like expenditure on management, distribution, administration, 
processing and purchasing, etc.; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the names of such items alongwith the 
possible cuts on each item; and 
(d) if no action has been taken in this regard the reasons therefor?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SOMPAL) 
(a) to (d): The main reason of continuous losses to Delhi Milk Scheme is the 
huge difference between me cost price and selling price of milk. At present, the 
average cost price of the processed milk of Delhi Milk Scheme (April, 98 to 
January, 99) is Rs.12.84 per litre (Toned in polypack) and Rs.11.59 per litre 
(Double Toned in polypack) whereas its selling price is Rs.7/- and Rs.6/- per 
litre respectively which was fixed by the Government in September, 1992. The 
same milk (Toned in polypack) is being sold by Mother Dairy @ Rs.13/- per litre. 
Apart from it, to contain the amount of losses, continuous possible efforts are 
made by the Ministry as well as by the Scheme. The possibilities to reduce the 
cost price of the milk are worked out constantly and are implemented to the 
maximum possible extent. It is obvious that the scheme will earn profit instead 
of loss, if the milk is sold at the rate equivalent to the price being charged 
by the Mother Dairy.

records.title: UTILISATION OF PERENNIAL RIVER WATER
details:
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE AND WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRI SOMPAL) 
(a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House.
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) to (e) OF STARRED QUESTION N0.227 
TO BE ANSWERED IN THE RAJYA SABHA ON 11.03.1999
The average annual flow available in rivers is around 1869 billion cubic metres. 
Owing to the topographic, hydrological and other constraints, the utilisable 
water resources is assessed at 1122 billion cubic metres, consisting of 690 
billion cubic metres of surface water and about 432 billion cubic metres from 
the annual replenishable ground water resources. Full utilisation of rain water 
is not possible due to topographical and environmental constraints, evaporation 
and vegetation losses and for allowing certain amount of water to flow in the 
river for maintaining the river regime.
The demand of water for various uses for the year 2000 is estimated as under:-
Sl. Use Water demand assessed fop 2000 A.D. No. Billion Cubic Meter 
1. Domestic 33 
2. Irrigation 630 
3. Industry 30 
4. Energy 27 
5. Other 30
Total 750
Keeping in view the future needs of water, the Government has taken various 
policy and programme initiatives. These include adoption of National Water 
Policy (1987), Command Area Development Programme, preparation of National 
Perspective Plan for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit 
areas, water management practices promoting efficient and economic use of water 
for various purposes, emphasis on water conservation through various methods 
including use of latest technologies and peoples` participation in management of 
water for diverse uses setting up of National Commission for Integrated Water 
Resources Development Plan in September, 1996 as well as launching of 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme since 1996-97 for expeditious 
completion of selected ongoing major and medium irrigation and multipurpose 
projects. Government is also promoting rain water harvesting and watershed 
management to replenish groundwater.
Planning, formulation and execution of water resources schemes is the 
responsibility of the State Government. Since the beginning of the Plan era, 
various steps have been taken for exploitation of available water resources. A 
number of small and large dams were taken up and as a result of this, the total 
live storage capacity has increased from 15.64 BCM at the beginning of plan era 
to about 177 BCM in 1995. Besides, an additional live storage capacity of 75 BCM 
will be created through dams under various stages of construction. In addition, 
dams under formulation/consideration will provide an additional live average of 
132 BCM.

details:
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE SHRI RAMAKRISHNA HEGDE) 
(a)to(d) : A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.
Statement referred to in reply to Parts (a)to(d) of Rajya Sabha Starred Question 
No.175 for answer on 8th March, 1999. Regarding `Export of Herbal Products`.
##
Under the Exim Policy 1997-2002 export of herbal products is freely allowed. 
Export of only certain species of plants, plant portions and their derivatives 
and extracts obtained from the wild has been prohibited. However, export of 
cultivated varieties of these species including their derivatives and extracts 
(including value added herbal formulations), except that of Red Sanders, is 
freely allowed subject to production of certificate of Cultivation from the 
designated authorities. List of such species of plants is available under 
Appendix 2 Schedule 2 of the book titled` ITC(HS) Classification of Export and 
import Items 1997-2002` which is a published document.
No maximum limit for export of such items has been fixed. Most of the species 
listed in the ITC(HS) Classification book are found as naturally growing stock 
in the wild and their cultivation outside the forest is almost negligible. It is 
for this reason that annual production and consumption of such herbs is not 
assessed and the data thereof is not maintained.

records.title: HARMFUL EFFECTS OF TERMINATOR SEEDS ON AGRICULTURE
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that foodgrain production by using the terminator seeds 
in agriculture sector in the country have proved damaging;
(b) if not, what is Government`s reactions thereto; and
(c) what risks are likely to be involved using terminator seeds in agriculture 
sector?
A N S W E R

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SOMPAL) 
(a)&(b): A patent on `Control of plant gene expression` US patent No.5723765 has 
been taken jointly by the Delta and Pine Land Company and the United States 
Department of Agriculture (USDA) for controlling the viability of seeds produced 
without adversely affecting the crop. This method is termed as `Terminator 
Technology`.
The seeds containing the terminator technology has not been allowed to enter 
into India through legal channels. Hence, its damaging effects on the country`s 
foodgrain production have not been tested. 
(c): The risks likely to be associated with terminator seeds in agriculture 
sector include: 
(i) the farmers will not be in a position to use seeds saved from the previous 
crop and will have to buy seeds for each sowing;
(ii) it will threaten the farmer`s expertise in seed selection and 
 traditional conservation methods of carrying forward the seeds; 
(iii) it will have implications on crop biodiversity.

details:

 during the last year had too much quantity of weed seeds;

 proves the substandard quality of wheat; and
(d) if so, the Government`s reaction thereto and whether the compensation for the
 loss have been received from the institute which is responsible for sending that 
substandard quality of wheat?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SOMPAL)
(a) Wheat imported from Australia during last year revealed presence of weed seed.
(b) The percentage quantity of weed seeds in imported wheat was 0.06% on weight basis.

records.title: SCHEME FOR DEVELOPMENT AND EXPANSION OF TEXTILE INDUSTRY .
details:
(a) whether Government have formulated any scheme to utilise modem techniques for 
the development and expansion of textile industry in the country;
(b) if so, whether Government have also formulated any action-plan regarding 
research and exploration of new techniques for utilisation of the textile 
industry in the country; and
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, me reasons therefor ?

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA) 
(a) to (c) There are 8 Textile Research Associations me functioning of which is 
jointly funded by Government of India, State Governments and industry. These 
Textile Research Associations generally undertake activities pertaining to 
Research and Development, providing services based on R&D including testing, and 
imparting technical education. They also carry out innovative work and render 
consultancy services to industry on various aspects of textile technology, 
including human resource development, and the application of scientific 
methodology in the textile industry to improve its technological performance and 
profitability. The research and services are intended also to reduce the costs 
and improve the quality and durability of fabrics, reduced pollution, conserve 
energy, utilise waste, and adopt new technology or improve existing 
technologies.
.Government has approved launching of Textile Upgradation Fund Scheme under 
which loans at applicable rate of interest would be available to the eligible 
textile and jute units. Under this Scheme, interest to the extent of 5%, 
interest points would be reimbursed to the lending nodal agencies (IDBI, SIDBI & 
IFCI) by the Ministry of Textiles.

records.title: DISTRIBUTION OF TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION FUND TO DIFFERENT SECTORS

power-loom industry and mill industry sectors from this fund for development of 
techniques; and
(c) the norms fixed by Government for envisaging this amount of share?

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA) 
(a)&(b): Government has decided to launch a Technology Upgradation Fund (TUF) 
under which units of the identified sectors of textile and jute industry would 
be eligible for loans from nodal agencies at an eligible rate of interest, the 
difference in rate of interest would be reimbursed by the Government to the 
nodal agencies concerned. No share has been fixed for any particular sector of 
textile industry such as handloom, power-loom or mill sector. 
(c): Does not arise.

records.title: CONSTRUCTION COST OF POWER PROJECTS .
details:
THE MINISTER OF POWER 
(SHRI P.R.KUMARMANGALAM)
(a) to (c) : The cost of the power plant depends upon its type, capacity site conditions, type of fuel, the detailed scope of the plant and the type of financing. While the completed cost for coal based thermal power plants recently cleared by CEA is of the order to Rs. 4.2 crores/MW the cost for naphtha based combined cycle plant cleared by CEA varies from Rs- 3.0 crores/MW to Rs. 3.5 crores/MW. The cost being cleared by CEA includes duties and taxes as well as high cost of financing. Further, the Indian ambient conditions lead to power output from the same plant particularly in case of Gas Turbine Plants. This further increases the cost of power plants per MW in India. The cost being cleared by CEA is the completed cost as installed including all civil works and all other infrastructural facilities required for construction of power plants such as external water system, external fuel handling system, fuel storage etc.
After allowing for all the factors mentioned above the cost of the power plants being cleared by CEA is comparable with the internationally quoted prices for the power plants which are in the range of Rs 2.0-2.3 crores/MW in case of combined cycle plants and Rs. 2.6- 3.5 crores/MW for coal based plants.

At times, though rarely, an organisation might also be found to be inadequately staffed due to increased workload etc. SUI studies of Ministries/Departments/Offices of the Government upto the end of the year 1997-98 had identified a surplus of 96,099 posts as against a total number of 6,46.175 posts covered by the studies. The SJSRY rests on foundation of Community Organisation-and Structure to provide supporting and facilitating mechanism for Local Development. The Community Development Societies (CDSs) to be set up under this programme would function as the nodal agency for implementation of the scheme. The SJSKY will be funded on a 75:25 basis between Centre arid States. The scheme consists of two special components viz. (a) Urban Self Employment Programme (USEP) and (b) urban Wage Employment Programme (UWEP). The USEP component gives special impetous to empowering arid uplifting the poor women and launches a special programme, namely. Development of Women and Children in Urban Areas (DWUA) under which groups of urban poor women setting up self employment ventures are eligible for subsidy upto 50% of the project cost.
Under this scheme no physical targets are fixed by the Central Government. The matter pertaining to the. physical targets under the scheme has been left to be decided by the State Governments in conformity with the guidelines of the scheme and result of beneficiary survey. details: Clubbed question in this member’s official feed

(a) whether it is a fact that a. number of cases of water dispute between the state of Punjab and Haryana are lying pending; if so, the details of these cases;
(b) whether Government have so far taken any measures to settle these cases;
(c) if so, by when and the details of the measures taken; and
(d) whet is the number of cases in which a final decision has since been taken alongwith the cases which are still under dispute?
ANSWER
THE MINSTER OF STAE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE(SHRI SOMPAL)
(a) A case pertaining to the Ravi and Beas water dispute is under consideration of Ravi & Beas Waters Tribunal.
(b) to 
(d) Since Punjab and Haryana, after re-organisation of Punjab could not arrive at an agreement on sharing of surplus Ravi and Beas waters within a stipulated period of two years, Government of India through a Notification dated 24th March, 1976 allocated shares of Punjab and Haryana and also that of Delhi, Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir in surplus Ravi-Beas waters. Punjab however, challenged the validity of this notification by filing suit in the Supreme Court. Efforts were thereafter made to resolve the issue and thus on 31.12.1981 an agreement was signed by the Hon`ble Chief Ministers of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan in the presence of then Hon`ble Prime

Minister of India. The issue pertaining to sharing of waters between Punjab and Haryana was reopened consequent to the signing of the Punjab Settlement on 24.7.85 (Rajiv-Longowal Accord). As a sequel to this settlement, Ravi and Beas Waters Tribunal (RBWT) was constituted by Government of India to inter-alia adjudicate the claims of Punjab and Haryana regarding their shares in the remaining waters. RBWT gave its report on 30.1.1987 setting out facts as found by it. Thereafter, the references of Central Government as well as of the State Governments of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan on the report of RBWT were forwarded to the Tribunal on 19.08.1987 for seeking explanation/guidance. The issue is still under the consideration of RBWT.

New Exploration Licensing Policy was approved by the Government of India in March`97. The main features of the policy are:
Allotment of blocks on open acreage system
Level playing field to National Oil Companies vis-à-vis private oil companies.
No blocks reserved for NOCs.
No compulsory participating or carried interest by national oil companies (NOCs).
International price of oil for discoveries made.
No payments of signature, discovery of production bonus.
No custom duty.
Freedom to sell crude oil and natural gas in domestic market at market related prices.
No cess on crude oil production.
Royalty payment on ad-valorem basis.
 12.5% for onland crude oil
 10% for offshore crude oil
 10% on natural gas both onshore and offshore.
Half the rate of royalty on production from deep offshore blocks for first seven years after commencement of commercial production.
Petroleum Tax Code to be in place.
Provision for Hydrocarbon Development Fund.
Beside, Govt. has given infrastructure status to E&P sector which allows 7 years Tax Holiday.

records.title: AIR POLLUTION MENACE .
details:
(a) whether it is a fact that the Centre for Science and Environment has observed in its report that 52,000 people in the country are losing their lives every year owing to air- pollution;
(b) if so, whether Government have assessed the abovesaid observations in the report; and 
(c) 
(c) if so, the reaction of Government thereon?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS
(SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI) 
(a) & (b) An article published by the Centre for Science & Environment (CSE), a non-governmental organisation, estimated that nearly52,000 premature deaths in 36 Indian cities have occurred in 1995 due to air pollution. There is no conclusive data to confirm these
figures.
c) The steps taken by the Government to reduce environmental pollution include the following:
1. The Government has formulated a comprehensive Policy Statement for Abatement of Pollution which envisages integration of environmental and economic aspects of development planning, lays
stress on preventive aspects of pollution, promotion of cleaner technologies to reduce pollution and health related aspects;
2. Fiscal incentives are provided for installation of pollution control equipment and also for the shifting of industries from congested areas.
3. Low lead petrol had been introduced in the four metro cities of Delhi, Mumbai, Calcutta and Chennai w.e.f. June 1994. Subsequently, unleaded petrol and catalytic converter fitted vehicles were introduced in the above mentioned 4 cities with effect from 1.4.1995;
4. The Government is implementing a major plan of action for introduction of unleaded petrol and catalytic converter fitted vehicles and introduction of low sulphur diesel for cleaner diesel vehicles in a phased manner. Fuel quality standards for petrol and diesel have been notified.
5. Gross emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emissions standards for all categories of new vehicles have been notified under the Central Motor Vehicles Rutes.1989 and are being enforced by the Departments of Transport of the various States.
6. For control of pollution from vehicles, emission norms for both petrol and diesel driven vehicles at the manufacturing stage were introduced for the first time in 1990 and made tighter in 1996. More stringent emission norms have also been notified and will come info effect from 1.4.2000.
7 Surveys have been conducted by the Central Pollution Control Board on the vehicular emissions in the major cities and towns in the country. The findings of the survey have been used for taking
mitigative measures,
8. The ambient air quality of various cities and towns are being monitored regularly through a network of 290 monitoring stations under the National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Program.
9. Emission from highly polluting industrial units and thermal power plants are regularly monitored by the Central Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards and action is taken against the defaulting units.
10. Emissions and ambient air quality standards have been notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

details:

(c) if so, what date has been fixed in this regard and if not the reasons therefor: and
(d) what steps have been taken to do away with the inconvenience
being caused due to delayed allotment of PAN ?
A N S W E R

MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(a) to (d) : A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT REFERRED IN REPLY TO PARTS (a), (b), (c) and (a) OF
RAJYA SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 26 FOR THE 1ST DECEMBER., 1998 `ON ALLOTMENT OF PERMANENT ACCOUNT NUMBER`. 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A total number of 1,51,07,026 applications for allotment of PAN have been received over the entire country as on 31.10.98. Targets have been fixed to allot PAN to these applicants 
(c) In Delhi Mumbai and Chennai all applications received `by the Regional Computer Centres were to be allotted Permanent account Number under new series by 31.10.1998 and all other applicants are to be allotted Permanent account Number through On-line System by 31.03.1999. In the rest of! the country 70%
of the applicants are to be allotted PN under new series by 31.03.1999. 
(d) With a view to avoiding inconvenience to the persons who had applied for allotment of Permanent Account Number and have not-yet been allotted the same under first proviso to Rule 114B a person is allowed to quote General Index Register Number till such time PAN is allotted to him. Further under third proviso
to Rule 114B any person who has not been allotted a PAN or who does not have a General Index Register Number and who makes a payment in cash or otherwise than by a crossed cheque drawn on a bank or by a crossed bank draft in respect of any specified transactions where quoting of Permanent account Number of General Index Register Number has been made mandatory he can make a simple declaration in Form 60 giving therein the particulars of such transaction.

(b) if not, the average rate of tariff of electricity for
industrial use in Spain, Germany, U.K., U.S.A., France, Canada, Italy, Sweden, Australia, Indonesia, Thailand and South Africa etc.; and
(c) to what extent it is more than that of in India and what is the average of electricity tariff in India?

THE MINISTER OF POWER ( SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM ) 
(a) to (c) : The average Power Tariff in the country is dependent upon its cost of supply, (cost of generation plus cost of transmission and distribution), electricity pricing laws and regulation. The cost of supply is dependent upon many factors such as technology, funding pattern, interest rate, hydro mix, price and source of fuel, completed cost, the geographical
area, load density, taxes and duties etc. These factors render comparability of the tariffs of different countries difficult.
